newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Moody's cuts Thailand foreign currency debt rating.
newsitem.headline: Moody's cuts Thailand foreign currency debt rating.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Wednesday it has downgraded the foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits of Thailand to A3 from A2.
As a result, all bonds of the Kingdom of Thailand had been downgraded to A3 from A2, the agency said in a statement.
Moody's said the downward adjustment reflected an incremental deterioration in the country's creditworthiness stemming from a number of factors, including:
(1) a build-up of short-term foreign currency obligations that has contributed to the recent escalation of the country's overall external debt ratios;
(2) structural problems that have adversely affected Thailand's competitiveness in its traditional manufactured export industries;
(3) constraints on the array and effectiveness of macroeconomic policies at the governemnt's disposal to respond to these challenges; and
(4) the crisis in the domestic financial and property sectors.
Moody's said however, the A3 rating continued to take into account Thailand's strong underlying fundamentals.

Foreign direct investment, attracted by the country's liberal trade and investment regimes and its favourable geographic locations, continued to take place and to drive Thailand's still robust rate of economic growth, it said.
In addition, such investment should be leading to technology transfers and to Thailand's ascent up the higher valued-added ladder of production.

Economic policy-making, though under some constraint, was guided by a conservative technocratic elite while a large cushion of foreign exchange reserves did provide some additional flexibility to weather severe shocks, it added.
Thailand's principal structural challenge going forward was its sizable call on foreign savings, as reflected in its large current account deficits, Moody's said.

The government aimed to contract domestic demand and to bloster the domestic savings rate in order to address this issue. Its main policy tool was fiscal tightening, and to this end the government has proposed cuts in its budget and in the budgets of states enterprises, the agency said.
In addition, forced savings schemes were being implemented in the public sector.

It said both measures, as currently framed, were promising developments that would help to address the chronic saving-investment gap -- although it was generally acknowledged that their scale would need to be deepened and sustained over time in order to make a significant impact.

Moody's noted that maintaining Thailand's domestic savings rate at its present level has become all the more challenging as one of its main components -- corporate sector savings -- was eroding under the weight of competitiveness problems, declining profits and high domestic interest rates.
Meanwhile, the household sector's saving rate has declined significantly over the past six years and was unlikely to rebound over the course of the medium-term.

The composition of government, traditionally based on a loose coalition of personality-centered parties, led to some risk that the necessary fiscal adjustments that were needed to deal with the country's foreign saving gap would be diluted or contravened, the agency said.
At the same time, there were limits to the effectiveness of monetary policy -- which must remain tight given the present configuration of the exchange rate regime.

Policy-makers might therefore be limited in the mix of policy prescriptions that could be used to resolve not only the current cyclical downturn, but also the long-term macroeconomic challenges, Moody's said.

The agency said Thailand required massive investments in infrastructure and human resource development in order to become competitive in higher value-added activities, for example. This would require not only increased domestic savings to accomplish, but also other coherent and forward-looking strategies that may challenge the capacity of the present political/administrative system.

Furthermore, the recent and rapid increase in the country's foreign currency debt burden -- Thailand's debt/exports ratio was already about 117 percent, well ahead of other A-rated sovereigns -- placed some additional constraints on the range of financing options available for continued development, the agency said.
It further noted that a large portion of the foreign currency debt had a maturity of less than two years.
In addition, financial and other stresses had not yet fully emerged in the current cyclical downturn. The financial sector was experiencing the negative symptoms of recent liberalization.
When coupled with an inflexible exchange rate regime, this had resulted in excessive and confidence-sensitive foreign capital movements, Moody's said.
In turn, this combination of policies had also led to a rapid rise in credit extended by both Thai banks and finance companies to the troubled property sector and to other speculative areas.
At this juncture, it was still too early to ascertain the magnitude of difficulties in the financial sector -- although they were expected to be protracted, it added.
Moody's said in its view, the level of uncertainty regarding the medium- and long-term outcomes warrant the one-notch rating reduction.
Addressing both the immediate and long-term challenges might prove far more painful and difficult than presently anticipated by many observers.
As a result, therefore, concerns about the sustainability of the corrective actions being implemented at this time were heightened by the reality of Thailand's over-dependence on foreign savings.
